Bioinformatics Resource Center - Rockefeller University" author: - "[http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_Agentic_AI/](http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_Agentic_AI/)" - "[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)" --- ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} # Responsible Use of AI for Coders: Skills? ::: ## Overview - [What is a skill? Why do we need it?](#what-is-a-skill) - [SKILL.md file](#skill-md) - [Installing skills from public sources](#installing-skills) - [Developing your own skills](#developing-skills) # What is a skill? Why do we need it? {#what-is-a-skill .center .middle background-color="#23373B"} ## Built-in commands and skills Most models will have commands that are built in and are always available when Claude Code or Codex are installed. These are part of the model and are explicitly called like a function call while coding. - e.g. `/init`, `/plan`, `/rewind`, `/compact` - [Claude code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands) and [Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/cli/slash-commands) have many common commands, and some unique as well. Skills are similar, but they allow for a high level of customization, are portable, and can be called by you or by the model. ## Skills help with reproducibility Investing in developing useful and well-designed skills can help your workflows in a few key ways: - consistency across analyses, increasing reproducibility and saving time - when you ask the model to do something, it does what you expect every time - shorter prompts without need for specific details - skills can be shared between people, providing standards within a lab, team, or between collaborators - extend capabilities of LLM model (e.g. Anthropic's built in word/excel skills) ## Skills are universal The skills format was initially developed by Anthropic, then the method was released as an open standard and is now used widely by most models. There will be slight differences between models that we will mention, but the concept is the same. The accepted specifications reference is here: [https://agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io). ## Skill directory A skill is simply a directory on your computer that the model knows about and will use when it thinks it should, or when explicitly called. - the *SKILL.md* file is the only required file in the skills directory. ```{=html} 
bioinformatics-skill/
├── SKILL.md          # Required: metadata (e.g. name, description) + instructions
├── scripts/          # Optional: code that can be run when skill is fired
├── references/       # Optional: documentation (e.g. method specifics, checklists)
├── assets/           # Optional: report templates, data files, images, etc.
└── ...               # additional files or folders
``` ## Skill scope The location of this folder will determine where that skill is available. - for global skills, with claude this will be located at *~/.claude/skills* - this will be slightly different for other models (e.g. *~/.codex/skills/*) - skills can also be limited to specific folders or projects. - a *.claude* or *.codex* directory can exist anywhere on your system, and your session will read any skill that exists in the path of that project. # SKILL.md file {#skill-md .center .middle background-color="#23373B"} ## SKILL.md file - YAML header The required *SKILL.md* file needs a YAML header and must have the `name` and `description` fields. A few [other optional fields](https://agentskills.io/specification) are allowed in the header as well (e.g. allowed-tools). - **name:** can only contain lower case letters, numbers, and hypens (no hyphens at the beginning or end of the name) - **description:** max of 1024 characters outlining what this skill does, and when the model should use it. ```{.yaml filename="SKILL.md"} --- name: bioinformatics-skill description: What does this skill do? When should it be used? --- ``` ## SKILL.md file - Body section After the metadata header, the rest of the SKILL.md file is markdown-formatted text providing instructions to the model. This can take many forms, but it might include: - steps in a workflow - expected outputs - common problems to avoid - when to run scripts in the skills folder - recommended to keep below 500 lines (~5k tokens) - more details or code templates can be selectively read from the *references* or *assets* folders - don't repeat things model already would know ```{.yaml filename="SKILL.md"} --- name: bioinformatics-skill description: What does this skill do? When should it be used? --- body: instructions for the model ``` ## Minimizing tokens with 'progressive disclosure' Skills are loaded and read into context in three steps: - **Discovery:** when a session is started only the name and description are read into context. - **Activation:** when the model determines a user prompt requires the skill, the rest of the SKILL.md file is read. - **Execution:** based on the instructions of the skill, additional files might be read or scripts might be run. This progression ensures that many skills can be available for use in a session, but your context isn't flooded with too much information and token use is minimized. ## A good description is key This format makes the description the critical part of the skill. It will determine whether a skill is used after a prompt is entered. If the description is too vague, then it will fire too often and use tokens unnecessarily. If it's too narrow, then it will never be used. Description tips: - should focus primarily on what the user is trying to do, and less on what the skill does internally. - explicitly say when it should be used: 'Use this skill when user asks to review, check, or QC scRNA analyses', not 'This skill performs QC for scRNAseq analyses' - including keywords you will often use will help ('review' or 'check' above) - can also include when it should not be used # Installing skills from public sources {#installing-skills .center .middle background-color="#23373B"} ## Installing skills - Public marketplaces - **Install from a marketplace:** Marketplaces contain plugins, each of which has their own set of skills. Anthropic and OpenAI have marketplaces with many useful plugins, but you can add a marketplace from any public source, like a Github repository (e.g. skills shared in your lab or by the BRC). ```{=html}
Marketplace
claude-plugins-official
Plugin
mattpocock-skills
tdd research code-review grilling
Plugin
skill-creator
skill-creator
Marketplace
your-lab-github
Plugin
lab-scrna-skills
qc-plots normalize cluster annotate-cells trajectory
Marketplace
rockefeller-brc
Plugin
brc-bioinformatics
MCP server
covered in a later lecture
``` ## Installing skills - Public marketplaces - **Install from a marketplace:** Marketplaces contain plugins, each of which has their own set of skills. ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} In the app or the CLI, you can just type in `/plugin` and navigate through the options to add first add a marketplace and then install a plugin. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ![](../imgs/plugin_menu.png){width=100% fig-align="center"} ::: ::: ## Installing skills - Public marketplaces - **Install from a marketplace:** Marketplaces contain plugins, each of which has their own set of skills. You can also do this explicitly on the command line. Claude Code: ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} # add marketplace from any github repository /plugin marketplace add / # e.g. anthropics/claude-plugins-official # install plugin from that marketplace /plugin install @ # e.g. skill-creator@claude-plugins-official ``` ::: Codex: ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} /plugin marketplace add / # add marketplace /plugin add @ # install plugin from that marketplace ``` ::: ## Installing skills - Single skill with npx - [**Install from a marketplace:** Marketplaces contain plugins, each of which has their own set of skills.]{style="color: grey;"} - **Add single skill with npx:** This essentially just copies in the skills directory to your computer where the model will find it. ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} npx skills find npx skills add / ``` ::: ## Installing skills- Security It is imperative that you trust the source where you install or add skills from. Remember that the entire skill and its associated files are potentially read and run on your computer. Many of your skills will likely be developed by you, but when it's not, its always important to read over all the files that come with a skill that you install. ## Popular plugin repositories - [https://github.com/anthropics/skills](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) - [https://github.com/mattpocock/skills](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills) - [https://github.com/obra/superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers) - [https://github.com/GoekeLab/awesome-genomic-skills](https://github.com/GoekeLab/awesome-genomic-skills): good resource for bioinformatics or science-focused skills # Developing your own skills {#developing-skills .center .middle background-color="#23373B"} ## Manually add a skills folder As we've discussed, a skill is at minimum a directory in an existing *.claude* or *.codex* directory that contains a SKILL.md file with a name, description, and body of instructions. ::: {.cell} ```{.shell .cell-code} # accessible to all projects on your system mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/bioinformatics-skill # accessible to only this project mkdir -p .claude/skills/bioinformatics-skill ``` ::: ## Built-in skill creators Both Claude code and Codex have skills that help guide you though making a new skill (`/skill-creator` for Claude). - As with any skill, they will usually be activated when you ask the model to make a skill (e.g. *I'd like to make a skill that reads in scRNAseq data and makes initial QC plots*) - These tools are designed to interview you to understand exactly what you want the skill to do. - The quality of the follow up questions depends on how well represented that type of action is covered in the model (scRNAseq will result in better interview set up than a more obscure method) - can also explicitly call the skill: `/skill-creator ` ![](../imgs/run_skill_creator.png){width=100% fig-align="center"} ## Building skills from your actual analysis In reality, your most useful skills will be made by the LLM, but are built from your actual analyses. The skill creator is designed to turn key discussion points within your session into facets of the skill. *e.g. Cell type X generally has higher mitochondrial reads, the starting threshold should be 10%, not 5%* This allows the model to identify packages you prefer, plot styles you like, important thresholds or quirks related to your studies, key decision points or edge cases, and to include this information in the skill. Specifics related to your work increases the value of a skill beyond just simply asking the model to do that task with no skill present. ## Smaller skills vs entire workflow as skill Generally it's better to have smaller skills that define discrete tasks as opposed to having one skill do an entire workflow or pipeline. ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} [✔]{style="color: #2e7d32;"} **Separate skills**
[*\*usually better*]{style="font-size: 0.6em;"} ```{=html} 
scrna-qc-skill/
└── SKILL.md 
scrna-clustering-skill/
└── SKILL.md 
scrna-de-skill/
└── SKILL.md
``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} [⚠]{style="color: #ef6c00;"} **Entire pipeline skill**
[*\*for fixed, standardized workflows*]{style="font-size: 0.6em;"} ```{=html} 
scrna-pipeline-skill/
├── SKILL.md          
└── references/     
    ├── qc.md
    ├── clustering.md
    └── de.md
``` ::: ::: ## Example of skill used in practice Here is the file structure of an example review skill. It is designed to detect the type of analysis and then use the guidelines **only for that method** by reading the relevant markdown file in the *references* directory. This allows for a univeral review skill that minimizes token usage by ignoring information for other methods. ```{=html} 
~/.claude/skills/bio-review
├── SKILL.md
└── references
    ├── bulk_rnaseq.md
    ├── clip_genelevel.md
    ├── cutrun.md
    ├── generic_code_quality.md
    ├── proteomics.md
    ├── riboseq.md
    └── scrnaseq.md
``` ## Example: bio-review SKILL.md ```{=html} ``` ```{=html}

Bio-Review Skill

Reviews a bioinformatics analysis script (R/Rmd or Python) at one of four effort tiers, combining a generic code-quality pass with a method-specific methodology/design/stats pass matched to the assay type being analyzed. The design/stats concerns in the reference files are language-agnostic — a confounded comparison, a mismatched imputation mechanism, or an MST trajectory artifact is the same problem whether it shows up in a Seurat/R pipeline or a scanpy/Python one. Only the concrete function/package names differ, and the reference files below list both where they diverge.

Step 1 — Determine the tier

Parse the skill argument for one of: simple, rigorous, fresh, thorough.

  • If none given, ask the user which tier they want rather than guessing — the token cost difference between tiers is large (see Step 4).
  • Tiers are defined in Step 4.

Step 2 — Identify the assay/method type

Look at the target file's library imports, function calls, and file/project naming to determine which reference file applies:

Signals Reference file
R: DESeq2, results(), dds, bulk count matrix, enrichGO/enricher/gseGO on a DESeq2 result. Python: pydeseq2 (DeseqDataSet, DeseqStats), gseapy (enrichr/prerank/gsea) on a DE result references/bulk_rnaseq.md
R: Seurat, Read10X/Read10X_h5, FindClusters, RunUMAP, scrublet/doublet detection, CellBender. Python: scanpy/AnnData (sc.pp.*, sc.tl.leiden/sc.tl.louvain, sc.tl.umap), scrublet, cellbender, scvelo, cellrank, palantir references/scrnaseq.md
R: DEP, limma on a protein abundance matrix, SummarizedExperiment with protein IDs, impute()/QRILC/MinProb/KNN imputation, Olink/mass-spec terminology. Python: a protein-abundance dataframe/matrix, sklearn.impute (KNNImputer/IterativeImputer), statsmodels-based moderated testing, Olink/mass-spec terminology references/proteomics.md
R: riboWaltz (bamtolist, psite, psite_info, frame_psite*, metaprofile_psite), ribosomeProfilingQC (estimatePsite, getPsiteCoordinates, assignReadingFrame), RiboProfiling, RiboseQC, ORFik; P-site / periodicity / reading-frame / RPF terminology. Python: plastid, RiboCode, ribotricer, riboviz references/riboseq.md
Gene-level CLIP-seq: CTK / CLIPflexR (tag2collapse.pl, ctk_tag2collapse, fq2collapse, stripBarcode), read names readID#copyNumber#barcode, *_uniq_clpsed.bed, STAR + samtools view -q 255 on CLIP, featureCounts on CLIP BAMs, "CLIP score" / CLIP_log2RPKM ~ RNA_log2TPM regression, BC filters, DESeq2 method (CLIP/RNA) interaction designs. Not peak calling / crosslink sites (nf-core/clipseq, PureCLIP, iCount, Paraclu, Piranha) — no checklist for those yet references/clip_genelevel.md
CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag terminology, IgG control, peak calling (MACS2/SEACR), spike-in normalization — these are CLI tools invoked the same way from an R, Python (subprocess/Snakemake), or shell wrapper script, so the same checklist applies regardless of the calling language references/cutrun.md

If the file mixes signals or none match clearly, ask the user which assay type this is rather than guessing — a wrong-method checklist gives false confidence.

Always load references/generic_code_quality.md regardless of assay type — it applies to every review.

These reference files are a floor, not a ceiling. Each one captures specific issues already confirmed against real scripts in this workspace — they are not a complete list of everything that can go wrong with that assay type, and cutrun.md in particular is an unvalidated draft. Always reason from general knowledge of the method (Seurat/DESeq2/limma/scanpy/DEP conventions, current best practices, known pitfalls not yet seen in any script here) in addition to the checklist, not instead of it. If the file being reviewed uses a tool or pattern the reference file doesn't mention at all, don't skip commentary on it just because it isn't written down — reviewing only what's listed would make the skill regress toward whatever was already caught before, instead of improving on it.

Step 3 — Static analysis only

State explicitly, every time (do not rely on this being inherited from context): no execution of shell/R/Python/etc. commands against real data — static analysis only — unless the user has explicitly authorized specific command(s) for this specific review. This applies to you directly and to any subagent spawned in fresh or thorough mode; restate it in every subagent prompt. A prompt-only "don't use Bash" instruction has proven leaky — subagents have still run read-only grep through Bash — so also tell them to search with the Read/Grep/Glob file tools instead of the shell, and report any shell use they admit to back to the user in the final summary.

Step 4 — Run at the requested tier

simple

Single pass, by you directly (no subagents). Read the file once, apply generic_code_quality.md only. Report obvious code errors, style inconsistencies, and anything that looks like it would error or silently misbehave. Skip method-specific design/stats commentary unless something jumps out. Fast, cheap — use for a quick sanity check.

rigorous

Single pass, by you directly (no subagents). Read the file, apply generic_code_quality.md and the matched method-specific reference file explicitly — walk its checklist item by item rather than skimming. Then go beyond the checklist: bring general knowledge of the method to bear on whatever the file does that the reference file doesn't cover. Give design/stats commentary (e.g. "is this comparison confounded," "does the imputation method match the missingness mechanism," "is multiple-testing correction applied consistently across sibling analyses"), not just correctness bugs. This is the default depth for a normal "review this file" ask.

fresh

One fresh, adversarial reviewer — a single subagent via the Agent tool (not Workflow), sitting between rigorous and thorough. The point is independence, not scale: the main agent has usually helped write or edit the code under review and carries the same assumptions and blind spots, while a fresh agent with no conversation history reads the file cold. Costs roughly one agent's worth of tokens instead of the dozens thorough can spawn.

  1. Before spawning, gather what the fresh agent can't know: the target file path(s); the matched reference file paths (~/.claude/skills/bio-review/references/...); sibling/upstream files worth cross-checking; and the settled decisions and already-known issues from project memory, so it doesn't re-flag deliberate choices (it may still flag a bug in how a settled choice is implemented).
  2. Spawn one agent whose prompt restates: static analysis only, file tools instead of Bash, no edits; the reference files are a floor, not a ceiling; an adversarial stance (it didn't write this code and should look for reasons it's wrong); and the evidence rules from Step 5. Tell it to read the whole target file, walk the reference checklists item by item, check correctness, method/design/stats and cross-file consistency, and then — before reporting — try to refute each of its own findings against the actual code (already handled elsewhere? intentional? misread?), dropping or downgrading any that don't survive. That self-refutation pass replaces thorough's per-finding verifier agents.
  3. Ask for structured output: per finding — title, file:line, severity (High/Med/Low), bug vs design call, checklist- vs general-knowledge-sourced, evidence, suggested fix, and what the refutation attempt found; plus a not-checked list and a verdict.
  4. Main agent's job afterwards: spot-check the top findings against the file before relaying (you have the context to catch a misreading quickly), say plainly where you disagree with the fresh reviewer and why rather than silently dropping its findings, dedupe, and present per Step 5 with a verdict. Report any shell use the agent admitted to.

Use fresh as the default when the user wants an independent second opinion on code that has been heavily edited in the current conversation.

thorough

Multi-agent, via the Workflow tool — only invoke this when explicitly requested (thorough), since it costs meaningfully more tokens than rigorous or fresh: the per-finding verify step means agent count scales with the number of findings (a 2026-09-28 run on one ~800-line Rmd used 49 agents and ~2.2M tokens). Prefer fresh unless maximum coverage is worth that cost. Structure:

  1. Find, in parallel — one agent per dimension: (a) code correctness, (b) method-specific methodology/design/stats (using the matched reference file as a starting point, explicitly instructed to also draw on general knowledge of the method beyond it), (c) cross-file consistency if this script has sibling files/templates (check the project directory for similarly-named files). Each agent prompt must restate the static- analysis-only constraint, restate that the reference file is a floor not a ceiling, and include the actual file content/path — a fresh subagent has no context otherwise.
  2. Verify, in parallel per finding — an adversarial pass on each finding from step 1: a second agent tries to refute it (e.g. "is this actually wrong, or is it intentional/already handled elsewhere in the file?"). Drop findings that don't survive.
  3. Report — combine surviving findings, most severe first.

Step 5 — How to present findings

Adopt an adversarial stance, especially at rigorous/fresh/thorough: you did not write this code and have no stake in it looking good. Your job is to find reasons it's wrong, not to confirm it looks reasonable. Actively try to refute the script's own implicit claims of correctness (a filter that's supposed to remove all NAs, a "this is idempotent" assumption, a comment claiming a step was already validated) rather than taking them at face value — re-derive a small example by hand where that's enough to check it.

Regardless of tier:

  • Every finding needs evidence: a file:line reference, the specific code/output it's based on, or a worked example — not just an assertion. "This looks wrong" is not a finding; "line 214 filters on padj but line 198 shows stat has no NAs in this dataset, so line 214 should use stat" is.
  • State what's actually wrong or worth discussing, with the file:line reference, not a restatement of what the code does.
  • Distinguish correctness bugs from design/stats judgment calls — a judgment call needs the user's input, not a fix.
  • If the user says they've already made a deliberate decision on something (e.g. "QC filtering is off for now"), don't re-flag it in future reviews of the same file unless they ask to revisit it — check project memory for previously-settled decisions before flagging something as an issue.
  • Any actual edit to the file (not just a finding) requires showing the diff and getting confirmation first — this is a hard rule in every project CLAUDE.md in this workspace, not just a preference.
  • When a finding comes from general knowledge of the method rather than anything written in the reference file, say so briefly (e.g. "this isn't in the checklist yet, but...") — that tells the user it's a newer/less battle-tested observation than a checklist-sourced one, and flags it as a candidate to fold into the reference file if they agrees it's real (see ~/.claude/skills/bio-review/references/ — update the relevant file directly when a new finding is confirmed, the same way the existing checklists were built).
  • State explicitly what you did not check and why (e.g. "did not verify the HPC path resolves — no execution access"), rather than letting silence imply full coverage.
  • For rigorous/fresh/thorough, close with an explicit verdict — PASS, PASS WITH CONCERNS, or FAIL — plus severity (High/Med/Low) per finding. If nothing real turned up, say so plainly; don't pad a clean review with generic praise.

Iterative reviews

If the user says they've edited the file since your last review and asks you to "reread and check again": re-Read the file — don't trust the version already in context. Confirm what's now resolved before reporting anything new, and watch specifically for edits that overcorrected or introduced a new inconsistency (this has happened before — e.g. fixing a universe bug by switching enricher() to enrichGO() but introducing a keyType mismatch in the same edit).

``` ## Time for an exercise Exercises are available [here](../exercises/exercises/Exercise_Skills_exercise.html).
